opus-5.5.text:
Einsum is a great starting point. In a sense, TensorLogic is what you get when you take einsum seriously and ask what else it is. But einsum is just one operation inside a framework that was designed for something else. In PyTorch or JAX it's a convenience function, a nicer way to write a tensor contraction. What it doesn't give you is a language, a single construct in which you can express all of AI.

The key observation behind TensorLogic is that a rule in logic programming, a Datalog rule, and an Einstein summation are essentially the same thing. Take a rule like "x is the grandparent of z if x is the parent of y and y is the parent of z." Represent the relations as Boolean tensors, and that rule becomes a join followed by a projection. The join is the product of the two tensors on the shared index y. The projection sums out y. Then you apply a step function so the result stays Boolean. That is an einsum with a nonlinearity on top. So the tensor equation is the one construct, and everything else falls out of it.

Here's what that adds beyond having an einsum function.

**First, it unifies the symbolic and the neural.** A layer of a neural network is a tensor equation. A logical rule is a tensor equation. Kernel machines, graphical models and transformers are all a handful of tensor equations. In PyTorch you write neural nets in tensors, and if you want reasoning you bolt on some separate symbolic system. In TensorLogic it's one language, so you don't have a neurosymbolic seam to glue together.

**Second, it brings over the semantics of logic programming, not just the arithmetic.** You get recursion, so you can define a relation in terms of itself, like ancestor in terms of parent, and the system computes the fixpoint. You get forward and backward chaining as inference strategies. In PyTorch, if you want transitive closure, you write a loop by hand and manage it yourself. In TensorLogic it's a declarative program, and the inference engine handles it.

**Third, it lets you reason in embedding space in a principled way.** Once rules are tensor equations, you can replace the objects with learned embeddings and the relations with tensors built from those embeddings. A temperature parameter then controls how the system reasons. At zero temperature it's purely deductive: exact, sound, no hallucinations. That matters a lot, because it's the thing LLMs can't guarantee. As you turn the temperature up, similar objects start borrowing inferences from each other, and you get analogical, generalizing reasoning. So you have a dial between rigor and generalization instead of being stuck at one end.

**Fourth, learning is native.** Because everything is a tensor equation, everything is differentiable. You can learn the parameters, the embeddings and, in principle, the structure of the rules themselves, which is predicate invention. That's something inductive logic programming always wanted and never scaled.

**Fifth, there's sparsity and scale.** Logic programs typically operate over huge, extremely sparse relations. Dense einsum in PyTorch is the wrong tool for that. A relational database join is the right tool, and in TensorLogic a sparse tensor and a database relation are literally the same thing. So you can compile either way: dense tensors on GPUs when that's efficient, database-style joins when things are sparse.

So the short version: einsum in PyTorch is an operation, and TensorLogic is a language built on the realization that this one operation, plus a nonlinearity, plus logic-programming semantics, is enough to express all of AI. PyTorch is to deep learning roughly what Lisp and Prolog were to symbolic AI. What's been missing is the language for AI as a whole, and that's what I'm trying to build.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that Einstein summation is already most of the way there, and that's precisely the point. The thing people miss is that einsum isn't just a convenient notation for contracting tensors. If you look at it the right way, it's a logical inference rule. A Datalog rule like "grandparent of X and Z if parent of X and Y and parent of Y and Z" is, literally, a join on Y followed by a projection, and a join followed by a projection is exactly what einsum does: you multiply along the shared index and sum it out. So the central observation behind Tensor Logic is that logic programming and tensor algebra are the same thing. One rule, one einsum.

But in PyTorch and JAX, einsum is just one op among hundreds. It sits inside an imperative Python program, surrounded by all this machinery that has nothing to do with the mathematics: control flow, mutable state, autograd bolted on from the outside, a type system that's really Python's type system. What Tensor Logic does is make the tensor equation the entire language. There's nothing else. Every program is a set of equations, each of which is an einsum followed by a nonlinearity, and the equations are themselves data, so you can reason about them, learn them, and compose them in ways you simply can't when they're buried in Python.

Three things fall out of that. First, you get symbolic reasoning and neural computation in one substrate. Logic programs, probabilistic graphical models, kernel machines, transformers, they're all just tensor logic programs with different choices of tensors. You don't need a neurosymbolic Frankenstein that bolts a theorem prover onto a neural net. Second, you get the ability to tune the temperature of your reasoning. At zero temperature, the sums behave like Boolean operations and you get sound deductive inference, no hallucinations, because the system can only derive what follows from what it knows. At higher temperatures you get the smooth, generalizing, analogical behavior of embeddings. Same program, same equations, you just dial the knob. That's something you fundamentally cannot express as an einsum call in PyTorch, because there the semantics are fixed. Third, the compiler can do things a deep learning framework can't, because it actually understands the structure. It can do query planning the way a database does, sparse and dense execution interchangeably, and automatic differentiation of the logical structure, not just the weights.

So the honest answer is: einsum is the atom, and Tensor Logic is the chemistry. The frameworks gave us the atom and then surrounded it with Python. We're saying throw away the Python and see what the atoms can do on their own.

astra-6.text:
Einstein summation gives you a very compact way to express tensor computations. What I want TensorLogic to add is a logical interpretation of those computations, so that the same language can express both a neural network and a set of reasoning rules.

Think of a relation as a Boolean tensor. If I say that Alice is Bob’s parent, that’s an entry in a two-dimensional tensor. Now take a rule: someone’s parent’s parent is their grandparent. You can express that as a tensor contraction over the intermediate person, using AND and OR in place of multiplication and addition. The shared index is also a shared logical variable.

The important point is not that PyTorch or JAX couldn’t execute that computation. They can. It’s that Einstein summation by itself doesn’t give you the abstraction of predicates, variables, and rules. TensorLogic is intended to make that connection explicit, so that learning and reasoning become things you can express and combine within one framework.

sol-6.1.text:
Einstein summation gives you a very compact notation for tensor computations. But by itself, it doesn’t give those computations a logical interpretation. What TensorLogic adds is the connection between tensor operations and logical rules: tensor indices can play the role of logical variables, and tensors can represent relations as well as numerical quantities.

So you can express something like “if X is a parent of Y and Y is a parent of Z, then X is a grandparent of Z,” and see how that corresponds to a tensor contraction. With Boolean operations, that’s logical inference; with numerical operations, you get the kinds of computations we use in machine learning.

The point isn’t just to give einsum a different syntax. It’s to have one language in which you can express both a neural computation and a set of reasoning rules, and compose them. PyTorch and JAX can provide the computational machinery underneath; the abstraction above that makes the relationships and rules explicit.
